surveyDefinition.title: Athletic Apparel — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on their exercise habits, purchase drivers, and product priorities in athletic apparel.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Athletes
segments.description: High-frequency exercisers (5+ times/week) who train for specific sports or fitness goals. They prioritize technical features like moisture-wicking, compression, and durability over style or price, and are willing to pay a premium for gear that enhances performance.

segments.name: Lifestyle Comfort Buyers
segments.description: Moderate exercisers (2-3 times/week) who value athletic apparel for its comfort and versatility in both workout and everyday settings. They are less concerned with cutting-edge performance tech and more with how the clothes feel and look for casual wear.

segments.name: Trend-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Individuals who are highly engaged with athletic apparel as a fashion category. They follow trends and influencer recommendations, prioritize style and brand image, and are willing to pay for the latest looks, even if they are less active.

segments.name: Value-Conscious Families
segments.description: Budget-focused buyers who purchase athletic apparel for themselves and their children. They are price-sensitive, prioritize durability and value for money, and are less loyal to specific brands, often shopping sales and multi-packs.

segments.name: Occasional Recreational Users
segments.description: Low-frequency exercisers (once a week or less) who own basic athletic apparel for light activities like walking or casual sports. They are not deeply engaged with the category, are price-sensitive, and rarely seek out new products unless their old ones wear out.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Athletic Apparel buyers in North America. It asks how people use Athletic Apparel, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Athletic Apparel for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased athletic apparel for personal use within the last 12 months; Individuals who exercise or play sports at least once a week; Ages 13-65 (with parental consent for minors). Excluded: Purchases made for resale or distribution; Team or corporate bulk purchases (e.g., uniforms for employees); Professional athletes purchasing as part of endorsement contracts.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy athletic apparel for personal use, pay for it themselves, and decide at the point of purchase (in-store or online). While some businesses may purchase uniforms or team gear, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly exercise or participate in sports (at least 2-3 times per week)
Value brand reputation and performance features (moisture-wicking, compression, etc.)
Follow athletic fashion trends and influencer recommendations
Purchase both online and in physical retail stores
Willing to pay premium for established brands (Nike, Adidas, Lululemon)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Activity & Usage Context
sections.covers: Establishes the respondent's exercise habits, the types of activities they engage in, and the role athletic apparel plays in their daily life.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Explores what triggers a purchase, where they shop, how much they spend, and the key factors that influence their choice of athletic apparel.

sections.label: Product Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Identifies the must-have attributes, quality cues, and the trade-offs respondents are willing to make between performance, style, sustainability, and price.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Future Intent
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction with current athletic apparel, identifies pain points and switching triggers, and gauges future purchase and recommendation intent.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey begins by establishing who the respondent is as an exerciser — how often they work out, what activities they do, and how they wear athletic apparel. It then moves into their shopping behaviour, exploring what triggers a purchase, where they buy, and what drives their choice. Next, it delves into their specific product requirements, including fit, sustainability, and the trade-offs they're willing to make. Finally, it measures their satisfaction with current gear, identifies pain points, and gauges their future loyalty and purchase intent. This arc cleanly separates the five…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Athletic Apparel in North America — who Individuals who have purchased athletic apparel for personal use within the last 12 months; Individuals who exercise or play sports at least once a week; Ages 13-65 (with parental consent for minors). The core consumer is an active individual who buys athletic apparel for personal fitness and lifestyle. This profile captures the primary decision-maker and payer, ensuring the survey reflects consumer preferences and behaviors.

segments.hypothesis: This group will report lower exercise frequency but high purchase frequency, will rank style and brand reputation as top drivers, and will be influenced by social media and celebrity endorsements.

segments.name: Value-Conscious Families
segments.description: Budget-focused buyers who purchase athletic apparel for themselves and their children. They are price-sensitive, prioritize durability and value for money, and are less loyal to specific brands, often shopping sales and multi-packs.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest price sensitivity, will prioritize durability and cost-per-wear, and will be more likely to purchase from mass-market retailers and discount stores.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp3 (days exercised per week) is the tie-breaker because it is the most direct behavioural self-report of exercise frequency, which is the primary discriminator between the performance-focused, lifestyle, and occasional segments.
notes: Weights are assigned only to options that clearly discriminate; many options are left unscored.
Each segment has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
Some options point to multiple segments only when the behaviour genuinely overlaps (e.g., running can be performance or occasional depending on frequency, but we kept it single to avoid dilution).
Trend-driven segment is reachable via style/trend triggers, purchase frequency, and trade-offs.
Value-conscious segment is reachable via price sensitivity, discount triggers, and durability concerns.
Occasional segment is reachable via low frequency and low engagement.
11 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey begins by establishing who the respondent is as an exerciser — how often they work out, what activities they do, and how they wear athletic apparel. It then moves into their shopping behaviour, exploring what triggers a purchase, where they buy, and what drives their choice. Next, it delves into their specific product requirements, including fit, sustainability, and the trade-offs they're willing to make. Finally, it measures their satisfaction with current gear, identifies pain points, and gauges their future loyalty and purchase intent. This arc cleanly separates the five…
storyline_notes: The segmentation lens combines usage frequency with jobs-to-be-done because athletic apparel serves both functional (performance) and expressive (fashion/lifestyle) needs, which are not captured by price sensitivity alone.
Added a dedicated 'Fit and sizing' beat in the product requirements section, as this is a critical and often frustrating aspect of apparel purchase that is not in the generic canonical arc.
Included 'Sustainability claims' as a distinct beat, reflecting the high environmental awareness in the North American market and its importance as a purchase driver.

The 'Purchase journey' section includes both 'Shopping channels' and 'Purchase frequency' to capture the omnichannel reality of the market and the replacement cycle, which is key for a consumable like apparel.

The 'Satisfaction' section includes a 'Friction points' beat to capture specific pain points like chafing or poor durability, which are common complaints in this category and help differentiate segments.
The 'Future intent' beat combines purchase and recommendation intent to efficiently capture both loyalty and advocacy in one narrative slot.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy athletic apparel for personal use, pay for it themselves, and decide at the point of purchase (in-store or online). While some businesses may purchase uniforms or team gear, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
